metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Degen v. United States

Opinion filed: 1996-06-10

Docket No.: 95-173

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 102
• 116 S. Ct. 1777
• 517 U.S. 820
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 3719

Case holding summaries:
• holding that a court in a civil forfeiture suit is not allowed to enter judgment against a claimant merely because he is a fugitive from a related criminal prosecution
• holding that a court in a civil forfeiture suit is not allowed to enter judgment against a claimant merely because he is a fugitive from a related criminal prosecution
• describing the fugitive disentitlement doctrine as "a rule forbidding all participation by the absent claimant" and "foreclosing consideration of claims on the merits"
• criminal defendants have no general right to obtain statements of Government witnesses before they testify
• "The extent of these powers must be delimited with care, for there is a danger of overreaching when one branch of the Government, without benefit of cooperation or correction from the others, undertakes to define its own authority."
• holding that defendant's flight from criminal prosecution did not justify disentitlement in related civil proceeding absent any impact on the course of such proceeding or the enforceability of any judgment therein
• "In an ordinary case a citizen has a right to a hearing to contest the forfeiture of his property, a right secured by the Due Process Clause."
• holding that the doctrine cannot be used to enter summary judgment in favor of the government in a civil forfeiture case
• holding that a summary civil forfeiture, approved without any hearing for the defendant under the fugitive disentitlement doctrine, violates a defendant's due process rights
• noting that in a civil case, "a party is entitled as a general matter to discovery of any information sought if it appears 'reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence'"
• "We have sustained, to be sure, the authority of an appellate court to dismiss an appeal or writ in a criminal matter when the party seeking relief becomes a fugitive."
• recognizing the 4 authority of appellate courts “to dismiss an appeal or writ . . . if the party seeking relief is a fugitive while the matter is pending”
• “A federal court has at its disposal an array of means to enforce its orders.”
• explaining that district courts have broad authority “to manage discovery in a civil suit, including the power to enter protective orders limiting discovery as the interests of justice require”
• noting that where dual citizen of U.S. and Switzerland remained in Switzerland and had not returned to face drug charges, “[t]he criminal trial cannot begin until he returns”
• "The extent of * * * [inherent] powers must be delimited with care, for there is a danger of overreaching when one branch of the Government, without benefit of cooperation or correction from the others, undertakes to define its own authority."
• "In many instances the inherent powers of the courts may be controlled or overridden by statute or rule."
• "We have sustained, to be sure, the authority of an appellate court to dismiss an appeal or writ in a criminal matter when the party seeking relief becomes a fugitive."
• "Disentitlement 'discourages the felony of 6 escape and encourages voluntary surrenders' and 'promotes the efficient dignified 7 operation' of the courts." (Quoting Estelle v. Dorrough, 420 US 534, 537, 95 S Ct 1173, 8 43 L Ed 2d 377, reh'g den, 421 US 921 (1975).)
• stating that "[p]rinciples of deference counsel restraint in resorting to inherent power"
• recognizing appropriate sanctions might be warranted against any uncooperative party if a civil litigant's failure to appear results in non-compliance with a legitimate order of the court respecting pleading, discovery, the presentation of evidence or other matters
• distinguishing the Court's holding that inherent powers did not support disentitlement in the circumstances of that case from the possibility that "enforcement of a disentitlement rule under proper authority" might be permissible
• "Therewould be a measure of rough justice in saying Degen must take the bitter with the sweet, and participate in the District Court either for all purposes or none. But the justice would be too rough."
• “A federal court has at its disposal an array of means to enforce its orders, including dismissal in an appropriate case.”
• "Principles of deference counsel restraint in resorting to inherent power,... and require its use to be a reasonable response to the problems and needs that provoke it...."
• noting courts have “certain inherent authority to protect their proceedings and judgments”
• noting that protective orders may be used "to prevent parties from using civil discovery to evade restrictions on discovery in criminal cases"
• holding that a summary civil forfeiture, approved without any hearing for the defendant under the fugitive disentitlement doctrine, violates a defendant’s due process rights
• noting that in a civil case, "a party is entitled as a general matter to discovery of any information sought if it appears 'reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence' "
• describing the purposes advanced by disentitlement as enforceability of a judgment, redress for the indignity visited upon the courts by an appellant's absence from the proceeding, and the need to deter flight
• "The Government has shown probable cause to forfeit the property, and [claimant] must refute the showing or suffer its loss."
• discussing application of the fugitive disentitlement doctrine
• recognizing the authority of appellate courts "to dismiss an appeal or writ ... if the party seeking relief is a fugitive while the matter is pending"
• declining to resolve the question whether Degen was a fugitive in all senses of the word where he had moved to Switzerland about one year prior to being indicted by a federal grand jury
